Still very much liking my purchase. Still rocking Merlin firmware. No issues with stability or performance.

Edit:

I have moved from the standard firmware to an open version, search for "ASUSWRT-Merlin" if interested. This has fixed my IP address issue as well as made several other improvements. The changes are too many to mention. That doesn't mean new features but bug fix's and so forth. However, if non stock firmware is not your cup of tea. ASUS rolls many of the fixs into its firmware from my understanding. So if you want to maintain more stock and less bleeding edge. Simply wait a bit longer and most of the changes will make it to you.

I am still very thrilled with my purchase.

The only thing I find meh is the antennas tend to be more floppy than I would like. However if you set it and don't get behind it monkeying around they stay just fine. I am sure many of us know the cord hell behind the entertainment center. This past go round I eliminated 90% of that and hopefully made it future proof. The only area still needing tweaking is behind my router. :(

Oh, I also turned off the smart connect feature. I was having issues with some of my iOS devices and its just easier for me to keep 3 separate SSID's and use them.
I maintain the following.
1 - 2.4 GHz for the IOT devices such as smart lights switches, older iOS devices of the kid's, etc.
1 - 5 GHz for all higher capable devices, media streaming devices so forth. Also configured as failover protection in devices that can support multiple configs and use ethernet first and wifi on failure of ethernet.
1 - 5 GHz for the wife's MacBook / iOS devices, my MacBook / iOS devices etc.

I am going to experiment using the smart connect more soon and see if the previous usage changes.

I purchased this to replace an aging Airport Extreme. I love the unit. It is easy to setup and the GUI is stable in Safari on OSX, Which I, often find other manufacturers have issues with. I had returned a competing product a week earlier as it had a security flaw. I could not be happier with my decision to spend the extra money. I generally believe you get what you pay for however, I was skeptical. So far it lives up to expectations and I think I received my moneys worth. It is a hefty sized unit. As for range, I have an older plaster walled home ( @ 1300 sq f) with metal mesh backing through out the home. Normally router signal don't play well, however the unit appears to reach all the corners of my home. I was using multiple Airport expresses as access point to fill in the holes so to speak. I have been able to turn off those units.

The only issue I had with the unit is the static IP is capped at 64 places. Additionally the GUI will take mac addresses as lower case. *Do not input the addresses using lower case.* It will prevent you from customizing the device name and the graphic. Once you remove the entry and re add it properly using upper case letters/numbers, you can easily customize the entry to your liking. This small issue is by no means a deal breaker for me. Its good points far out weigh its few issues.

text_fidelity_a:
TV Antenna - 1byone Amplified 50 Mile HDTV Digital Antenna Powerful Amplifier Signal Booster for All TV 4K UHF VHF 1080P Local Channels with 20ft Coaxial Cable This is a review of the 50 mile OUS00-0562 model. To summarize: It works. But it's no better than my cheap [[ASIN:B000HKGK8Y RCA Indoor FM and HDTV Antenna]] antenna that I was trying to replace, yet costing several times more.

With my cheap RCA "rabbit ears" antenna I was getting 18 channels, being 8 miles away from the transmitter. According to my digital-to-analog converter most TV signals were in the range of 75% to 30%. I was looking for a better antenna to improve the signal quality, so when I saw that the OUS00-0562 model was on sale I bought it. I didn't believe the 50 mile claim of this antenna since most antennas with this claim are large, more expensive and rather directional. But I figured that even if it was half that it had to be better than my RCA one. Whatever this antenna was directional of not was not specified, I assumed that it was not.

The OUS00-0562 model comes with an antenna with a 20 foot non-removable cord. This was disappointing, but I should have realized this when looking at the product pictures. Having so much cable slack is a waste when it sits 3 feet from the TV. Before I installed the 1byone antenna I took note of signal strength of each channel of my RCA antenna. The OUS00-0562 package also comes with an amplifier, which I connected to my RCA antenna as a test - and was disappointed. Only 3 channels were 10% higher, and that was within margin of error. The OUS00-0562 disappointed me soon after, as there was no change in signal strength on any channel over the RCA antenna (except that it gave me two more channels at 40% signal).

The short version:

RCA "rabbit ears" - 18 channels, 75%-30% (+/- 5%)
RCA "rabbit ears" with 1byone amplifier - 18 channels, 70%-30% (+/- 5%)
1byone OUS00-0562 with 1byone amplifier - 20 channels, 70%-30% (+/- 5%)

I tried to reposition the OUS00-0562 antenna to see if there was a directional issue, if I was out of the "sweat spot." I did notice 5-10% dips here and there but no marked improvements. I didn't spend much time on this and since it wasn't shipped with a stand. You can buy one, but I didn't want to spend any more money on it since to me it was overpriced as is. I promptly returned it.

I will give this antenna one point though. It's better looking than the RCA antenna and it takes up less space. So if looks and space matter, it might be for you.
text_fidelity_b: TV Antenna - 1byone Amplified 50 Mile HDTV Digital Antenna Powerful Amplifier Signal Booster for All TV 4K UHF VHF 1080P Local Channels with 20ft Coaxial Cable

text_fidelity_a:
ELECOM Relacon Handheld Trackball Mouse, Thumb Control, 2.4GHz Wireless, Ergonomic Design, 10-Button Function with Smooth Tracking, Windows11, MacOS (M-RT1DRBK) I've bought and currently use both variants of the Relacon mouse. I'm putting this review on the wireless version.

Overall, 5 stars for the wireless with dongle, 3 stars for the Bluetooth. Unfortunately the Bluetooth one is a bit choppy with tracking, causing the pointer to jump to a random place on the screen often enough to be annoying. The dongle one doesn't have this issue for me. Otherwise they're identical in function and feel.

As a dedicated thumb trackball user since the early 90s, I love it! It is much better quality than any other ambidextrous thumb trackball I've optimistically tried over the years when looking for an alternative to the standard right (or rare left) dedicated handed thumb trackball. I have never been able to get comfortable or quick with finger trackballs, no matter how much I have wanted to or worked at it. Same with the Thinkpad trackpoint.

It is a physical relief to have a mouse that I can use in a neutral wrist position without having my hand or arm stretched out. It is especially nice to be able to transfer and use the mouse with my left hand when I need to type or do something else with my right.

I haven't installed the software or tried to remap the buttons. I just plug in the dongle or pair with Bluetooth, and Windows recognizes it. Since my displays are 1080 or smaller, I keep the speed or acceleration or dpi setting at 1 blink. The button is below the power switch, so I do accidentally tap it occasionally, but it's quick and easy to cycle back to 1.

The stand is more stylish than functional, and even with practice the mouse will sometimes slide right off, but at least it's included. Most of the time, I just switch it off and set the mouse on its side.
text_fidelity_b: ELECOM Relacon Handheld Trackball Mouse, Thumb Control, 2.4GHz Wireless, Ergonomic Design, 10-Button Function with Smooth Tracking, Windows11, MacOS (M-RT1DRBK)

text_fidelity_a:
Kingston 64GB DataTraveler Elite G2 Black Metal Casing Fast 180MB/s R, 70MB/W USB 3.1 Flash Drive with LED light indicator (DTEG2/64GB) This is an unremarkable USB drive, with unexciting performance, for an unattractive price. (That's pretty much it for the substance of the review.)

I do my tests on a pretty fast computer with tons of memory, and an SSD system drive, while I'm doing nothing else on the computer, so no system resource constraints should affect the results. I test writes from SSD to USB, and reads in the other direction. I also use a set of 2GB test files, so that I get true results (small files can give misleading results).

I saw writes to the USB drive going between 4.5 and 8 MB/s, which is really pretty slow. I can get 16+ consistently on a little Lexar 32GB drive I have lying around. And a quick look in Amazon shows that I can find much faster USB3 drives for a bit less or a bit more, promising about 5x the write performance.

Finally, the form factor is terrible. This is a big fat ugly drive, you can get higher capacity and much better performance in slim little drives, including nano-drive size products.

Bottom line, it's ok, but I can't recommend it.
text_fidelity_b: Kingston 64GB DataTraveler Elite G2 Black Metal Casing Fast 180MB/s R, 70MB/W USB 3.1 Flash Drive with LED light indicator (DTEG2/64GB)

Zinwell ZAT-970A Digital to Analog TV Converter Box (for Antenna Use) We needed to save some money, and I'd heard that Over The Air broadcasts included channels you wouldn't otherwise get. My Dish TV account provided local channels and a whole bunch of channels I didn't use; but the OTA feature really helps!

I paired the Zinwell digital / analog converter box (highly rated, outstanding Amazon price) with the Radio Shack Antennacraft® HDX1000 Amplified HDTV Antenna (also highly rated). You should know one thing -- the mast size for the Dish TV is larger than the mast size for the Antennacraft antenna, so you can't just remove the Dish and replace it with the Antennacraft on the same mast. But it is an easy install.

As a trial, before going up to the roof (2 story house), I set the Antennacraft in the downstairs window that has a view to the southwest (the direction our local TV stations broadcast from). Without the Zinwell, you're limited to the low power analog stations (mostly Spanish language, a few home shopping stations). I think I got about 6 stations. Then I plugged in the Zinwell in line between the antenna and the TV (after disconnecting the Dish TV feed), did a scan, and had 20 channels. Repeated the process upstairs (remember, we have a 2 story) and had 22 channels!! All the local tv stations (NBC, ABC, CW, ION, PBS, etc.) that broadcast digitally came through great!! Unfortunately, it started raining :( so after the rain stopped, I only got as far as getting the mast installed outdoors before it got too dark. It won't take long to finish.

Only one Zinwell related item: You're supposed to be able to choose the feed from the Zinwell to the TV to be either Coax or the Composite (yellow video, red and white audio). I couldn't get the composite to work in setup, but the coax worked just fine. Haven't had a chance to see if, once programmed, the composite would work, or if for some reason I hooked it up to my tv incorrectly (hard to imagine), but ... since the coax works so well, and video and audio quality are great, I'm money ahead and not complaining!!

So when do I break even? $80 antenna plus 2 $40 boxes = $160; Dish TV was costing me about $55/month (yeah, once you've been a subscriber for a while, there's essentially no customer retention policy, so, good by Dish!! -- and that's probably true for Directv and Comcast, too). So after 3 months, essentially at the start of January, I'm home free!! Thanks, Amazon, you're helping me save money, and that's really great!!

NOTE: I only ordered one Zinwell to test out things, now I've ordered a second for our other TV (didn't want to put too much at risk if it didn't work, but it works great!).

NOTE 2: The gov't coupon program is long dead, no hope of getting $40 off on one, just be glad if you waited that these things are as reasonably priced as they are.
text_fidelity_b: Zinwell ZAT-970A Digital to Analog TV Converter Box (for Antenna Use)

UltraPro 8K HDMI 2.1 Cable, 6ft. High Speed 48Gbps, 8K @ 60Hz, 4K 1440p 1080p @ 120Hz, HDR VRR eARC QMS, Compatible with PS5 Xbox Series X Roku TV, Streaming, TV, Monitor, All HDMI Devices, 57347 Note: the 4K term is marketing, just about all consumer devices are UHD (2160p). So I'm going to use the UHD term, feel free to translate to "format commonly referred to as 4K" if you prefer.

I tested this cable on my newest UHD tv, with streaming UHD video from multiple sources, and then with a UHD nature documentary on a bluray player. I'd been using a very good 18Gb ("4K") cable before, so possibly a side-by-side test wouldn't show any difference. But I did immediately notice how sharp and bright the picture was in both cases, so I can at least say that this makes a very good video cable for UHD.

The cable is well made and feels sturdy, with a nice grab handle at each end, and inserts just the way it should into HDMI ports, with neither wiggle nor overmuch tightness. I didn't notice any minor flaws that might make me concerned about build quality, and I would expect it to last, at least until it becomes obsolete.

What should you buy if you don't have any so-called 8K media or devices, like most of us, and don't see them in your immediate future? In that case I'd just go with very good "4K" or "8K" cables, but without paying premium prices. The product description might say "Premium High Speed HDMI Cable" (18Gbps) or "Ultra High Speed HDMI Cable" (48Gbps). The first corresponds to the HDMI 2.0b standard, the second to HDMI 2.1.

text_fidelity_a:
TCL 32S3800 32-Inch 720p Roku Smart LED TV (2015 Model) Update: After less than 60 days of owning the TV, the ENTIRE audio panel died. None of the external audio ports work anymore for no reason whatsoever. Worked fine, then boom just stopped working. Thought it was my soundbar, so I bought a new soundbar, but nope, soundbar works just fine when connected to the cable box. Amazon Prime was awesome in helping me return it, and I'll be picking up a more reliable brand. When it came time to purchase a new TV we approached it the same way we approached buying a house. We made a list of the features we wanted (a SmartTV with Wifi, streaming channels, Amazon Prime, 40” and affordable at around the $250 mark). After looking at our options in terms of price and convenience, we decided that it made the most sense to purchase it through Amazon Prime.

After much research, we decided that the TCL TV’s offered the best value, met our budget requirements, and our decision to purchase the TV through Amazon enabled us to purchase the TV with interest free financing over 6 months.
Appearance.
The TV came in a large box with the stand hardware: remote, power cable and batteries plus simple instructions that were in separate bags. You do not get a HDMI or any other cables. The TV has a simple non-fussy design with approximately half inch bezel all around. The stand that comes with it is simple and screws on with two screws at each side. The stand footprint requires about 8.5 inches of depth to stand on. I like that the stand is low profile raising the screen about 2” above the surface it is standing on.

Setup

The old analog phono inputs are on the back and quite hard to reach once the TV is up on the mantle and they protrude straight out the back which would require more space between the wall and the TV if you use them. The power cable plugs into a recessed area low down on the left side and doesn’t interfere with the location of the tv. All the modern input and output sockets are behind the screen on the right side about 8 inches back. We don’t use any subscription TV service; just a double bowtie antenna mounted on one of the gutter pipes at the back of the house. The coaxial input for the antenna along with three HDMI ports, an optical input, 3.5mm jack and USB socket are all here. We use two of the HDMI sockets one for the 1TB Media hub and the other for our notebook.

Once everything is plugged in and turned on. The TV introduces you to the basic setup process. It takes less than five minutes to find your way around. The remote is minimalist with the most basic controls on the front (Volume Up/Down toggle and mute buttons on the side). It’s small, unfussy and easy to use. The UI for the TV is not flashy but functional and easy to navigate. Setting up WIFI, registering your TV and introducing you to streaming channels and how to add them to your desktop are covered quickly and then you are left to your own devices.

Since we are just using an antenna we were initially a little apprehensive. Wondering how well that would work, or even if the TV had a tuner since everyone seems to use dish or cable these days. It has a tuner that works flawlessly. We managed to pick up almost 3 dozen channels many of them HD. A quick look online showed us a map of where the broadcast towers are and helped us aim our antenna for best reception.

In use.

The TV has a really nice clean picture and since it is an LED TV where a grid array of LED's light the screen uniformly rather than a couple of fluorescent lamps there is practically no limit to the viewing angle. The screen is not high gloss and prevents reflection and most glare from bright light sources. When turned on a non invasive 3” horizontal strip of illuminated plastic at the bottom shows you the TV is powered on. It flashes during startup and goes out when the screen is illuminated.

Image

Image quality is excellent BUT on initial setup it is on a bright echo setting. Which is very high contrast and overly saturated. I guess it is a power saving mode (claimed 16 watts) but it is a bit stark and overwhelming and shows some dithering on smooth color transitions as though it is running at a lower bitrate with fewer colors. When turned to theater mode the quality of the picture is MUCH better with very smooth transitions on subtle colour gradients.

Sound

Sound is similar. Like most LCD style TV’s this one comes with tiny speakers. Again the default sound setting seems to be very flat. Probably to conserve energy. There are about four presets and again we went with theater which gives the broadest range and warm midtones without overdoing the bass. It doesn’t sound too bad and is not thin and reedy like the default setting.

Smart TV functionality.

We originally wanted WIFI because as Amazon Prime members we get a lot of free on demand media. This is similar to Netflix where you can watch a huge catalog of TV and movies for free, buy or rent them for a small fee. The same goes with music. This worked perfectly.

What we weren’t expecting was the sheer volume of streaming media available for free via WIFI. There are hundreds of channels, many of them free to choose from, many mainstream ones that let you view their current episodes of popular shows on demand when you want to watch them. You can also sign up for pay for view services like HBO and showtime individually.

One nice thing is that the TV has a global search option. You can search for anything by title, director, actors name, character, keywords and the TV will find everything relating to your search and list what is available by channel. So you can easily pick out what you want to see.

Mobile devices and streaming from those devices

There are apps for Android and iOS as well as Windows. I was able to control the TV from all our devices. In many ways it is more responsive, especially if you need to type in text. If you have media on your PC there are Apps for the TV that will let you stream from your phone, notebook, desktop computer etc.

Streaming from those devices tends to work ok. I did find that the TV’s built-in media player was a little limited in supported data formats. Setting up our digital media hub with its own channel was very easy and luckily our Western Digital media hub has far more extensive support for many of the more exotic file formats like FLAC lossless digital audio. And other formats are more often limited to computers. The TV does support the more mainstream formats like mp3, mpg, jpg etc.

Conclusion

For us, this TV proved to be a very good and affordable purchase. Especially when you factor in the 6 months interest fee financing Amazon offers prime members. We did sign up for a free month of Netflix too. The remote has a dedicated Netflix and Amazon streaming button. But we were not that impressed with Netflix when our Amazon Prime membership offered all the same features and more thanks to the addition of Amazon Prime music.

When you combine all this TV’s features with our media hub and Amazon Prime we are a bit overwhelmed with the sheer amount of stuff out there to watch. Even if we had no antenna and just a WIFI internet connection. The vast number of free streaming HD channels is extensive making the need for TV subscription plans pretty much obsolete unless you have a very specific need.

We really like this TV and highly recommend it.
text_fidelity_b: TCL 32S3800 32-Inch 720p Roku Smart LED TV (2015 Model)
